abstract: Introduction: Symbiodiniaceae dinoflagellates are essential for coral juvenile development and survival, yet early-life symbiont provisioning remains underused in coral restoration. Objectives: We tested whether inoculating sexually propagated Acropora spathulata recruits with cultured symbionts before reef deployment improves survival and shapes symbiont community composition. Methods: Recruits inoculated with cultured Cladocopium sp. (C1) or Durusdinium trenchii (D1), and uninoculated recruits (Control) were deployed on the central Great Barrier Reef. Results: Both inoculation treatments approximately doubled survival relative to Control, although the benefit varied with local benthic habitat. C1 and D1 recruits were dominated by symbiont sequences matching their respective inoculated cultures, while Control recruits predominantly harboured a Durusdinium-dominant community closely resembling the cultured D1. Cultured C1 was also dominant among most C1-inoculated recruits after nine months, although some diverged from the inoculated community towards a mixed assemblage with Durusdinium. Conclusions: Similar survival benefits in the two inoculation treatments suggest that the timing and success of symbiont establishment were more critical for early survival than symbiont genus identity, under the conditions and period of this study.
